content.title: About
content.content: The pork, rice and cheese burrito is a Mexican dish consisting of a large wheat tortilla wrapped around a filling of tender pork, seasoned rice and melted cheese. It provides a balanced mix of protein, carbohydrates and fats for sustained energy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Burritos originated in northern Mexico where wheat flour is more common than corn.
Pork is often marinated in chipotle, coriander and lime, giving it a smoky flavor.
Mexican rice is typically cooked with tomato sauce and turmeric, which adds color and taste.
The cheese used is usually a blend of cheddar and Mexican “queso” that melts smoothly.
Burritos are commonly served with salsa, guacamole and sour cream, allowing diners to adjust spiciness and creaminess.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Pork supplies high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Energy‑rich carbohydrates
items.content: Rice provides complex carbs that release energy slowly, helping you feel full longer.

items.title: Calcium and phosphorus
items.content: Cheese contributes calcium and phosphorus, important for bone health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both pork and rice contain B1, B3 and B6 vitamins that support metabolic processes.

items.title: Dietary fiber (if whole‑grain rice is used)
items.content: Whole‑grain rice adds fiber, aiding digestion and blood‑sugar control.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: The cheese and pork can make the burrito calorie‑dense; watch portion sizes if weight management is a goal.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Salt used in the pork rub and cheese can increase sodium intake, which may be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Digestive heaviness
items.content: A rich meat and cheese filling can be heavy for those with sensitive stomachs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Burritos are hand‑held; cut them in half for easier handling. Warm them in a microwave or skillet until the cheese melts. Top with fresh salsa, guacamole or sour cream to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store prepared burritos in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, wrap tightly in plastic and freeze for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Fish and vegetables is a dish centered on tender fish (such as cod, salmon, or sea bass) baked or steamed together with a variety of vegetables like zucchini, bell pepper, cauliflower, spinach, peas and others, excluding carrots, broccoli, dark‑green leafy greens, potatoes and tomato‑based sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fish is an excellent source of omega‑3 fatty acids that support heart and brain health.
Steamed vegetables retain most of their vitamins and minerals.
The tradition of pairing fish with vegetables dates back to Mediterranean cuisine, where such meals are considered a cornerstone of a healthy lifestyle.
Preparing the dish without tomato sauce allows the natural flavors of fish and vegetables to shine.
A colorful mix of vegetables makes the plate appealing and nutrient‑dense even without bright red ingredients.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Fish provides complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: EPA and DHA help reduce inflammation and support cardiovascular function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both fish and vegetables supply B12, B6 and niacin, important for metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish contains iodine, selenium, magnesium and potassium, which aid thyroid function, immunity and electrolyte balance.

items.title: Fiber and antioxidants
items.content: Vegetables such as zucchini and bell pepper are rich in dietary fiber and antioxidants that promote digestive health.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to seafood, ranging from skin rashes to severe anaphylaxis.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Certain fish species can contain mercury or other heavy metals; choosing smaller species and reputable sources reduces risk.

items.title: Vegetable digestion
items.content: People with sensitive stomachs may find raw or undercooked vegetables hard to digest; cooking them until tender is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, garnished with fresh herbs (parsley, dill) and a squeeze of lemon. Fish can be portioned into fillets, while vegetables may be left in larger pieces or chopped, according to preference. It works well as a standalone meal or alongside whole‑grain sides such as quinoa or bulgur.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked fish and vegetables in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze portions for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: The vegetarian hot dog is a plant‑based alternative to the classic hot dog, made from soy protein, wheat gluten and a blend of spices. It delivers the smoky, savory flavor of a traditional sausage without any meat, making it suitable for vegetarians and those reducing meat consumption.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Vegetarian hot dogs often use textured vegetable protein (TVP) derived from soy to mimic the meat‑like texture.
They come in a variety of flavors: classic smoked, spicy chili, barbecue, and even cheese‑infused.
Many brands fortify the product with B‑vitamins and iron to replace nutrients typically obtained from meat.
Vegetarian hot dogs are packaged in the same way as conventional ones, allowing an easy swap in recipes.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with meat counterparts, vegetarian hot dogs contain less saturated fat, which can support heart health.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Soy protein provides all essential amino acids, helping maintain muscle mass.

items.title: Rich in fiber when served with whole‑grain bun and veggies
items.content: Adding a whole‑grain bun and fresh toppings boosts dietary fiber for better digestion.

items.title: Cholesterol‑free
items.content: Absence of animal ingredients makes it virtually cholesterol‑free.

items.title: Contains iron and fortified B12
items.content: Some brands add iron and vitamin B12, nutrients important for vegetarians.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: People allergic to soy should avoid this product.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Certain varieties are high in salt; check the label if you watch sodium intake.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: If wheat gluten is used, the product is not suitable for those with celiac disease.

items.title: Processed ingredients
items.content: Like many convenience foods, it may contain preservatives and flavor enhancers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the hot dog in a pan, microwave, or on a grill, place it in a bun and add your favorite toppings: mustard, ketchup, pickles, sauerkraut, or avocado.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 0 °C–4 °C in the original packaging for up to 5 days after opening. Freeze in an airtight bag for up to 3 months. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or strange appearance.

content.title: About
content.content: Romaine lettuce is a crisp, leaf vegetable belonging to the Asteraceae family. It features long, slightly wavy leaves with a firm, light‑green core. Raw romaine is commonly used in salads, sandwiches, and as a side because of its mild, slightly nutty flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Romaine is considered one of the most nutrient‑dense lettuce varieties due to its high vitamin and mineral content.
Its name derives from the ancient Roman city of Rome, where it was cultivated in antiquity.
Leaves can grow up to 30 cm long while the core remains crunchy even after light cooking.
Romaine lettuce is the classic base for Caesar salad.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: A 100‑g serving provides over 100 µg of vitamin K, essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: High in vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene in the leaves converts to vitamin A, supporting vision and immune function.

items.title: Source of folate
items.content: Folate is needed for DNA synthesis and is especially important for pregnant women.

items.title: Low‑calorie fiber source
items.content: One cup of shredded romaine offers about 2 g of dietary fiber, aiding digestion and satiety.

items.title: Contains potassium and magnesium
items.content: These minerals help regulate blood pressure and support muscle function.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Raw leafy greens can harbor Salmonella or E. coli; thorough washing before consumption is recommended.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Conventional farming may leave pesticide traces; choosing organic romaine reduces this risk.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience leaf‑vegetable allergies, resulting in itching or swelling.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Romaine lettuce can be eaten raw in salads, added to sandwiches, used as the base for Caesar dressing, or lightly grilled. Before serving, rinse the leaves well and pat dry.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store romaine in the refrigerator in a bag with a slight moisture or in a container lined with a paper towel. It stays fresh for 7‑10 days when kept cold. Remove any wilted leaves to extend shelf life.
